course.title: Genetics
course.description: How traits are stored in DNA, copied, shuffled by meiosis, and passed on — from Mendel's peas to CRISPR. Structure adapted from the Genetics unit of OpenStax Biology 2e (CC BY 4.0).

questions.prompt: DNA's double helix is held together by base pairs. Adenine (A) always pairs with…
questions.explanation: A pairs with T, and G pairs with C — see 'DNA structure & replication'.

questions.prompt: A gene is best described as…
options: a segment of DNA that codes for a product
questions.explanation: A gene is a stretch of DNA carrying instructions for a product — see 'Genes, chromosomes & mutations'.

questions.prompt: In a cross of two heterozygotes (Aa × Aa), the phenotype ratio of dominant to recessive is…
questions.explanation: A monohybrid Aa × Aa cross gives a 3:1 phenotype ratio — see 'Mendelian inheritance'.

questions.prompt: Meiosis produces gametes that are…
options: haploid, with half the chromosome number
questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number to make haploid gametes — see 'Meiosis & genetic variation'.

questions.prompt: During protein synthesis, DNA is first copied into…
questions.explanation: Transcription copies DNA into mRNA — see 'Transcription & translation'.

questions.prompt: In RNA, which base replaces thymine (T)?
questions.explanation: RNA uses uracil (U) instead of thymine — see 'Transcription & translation'.

questions.prompt: A homozygous individual for a gene carries…
questions.explanation: Homozygous = two identical alleles (e.g. AA or aa) — see 'Mendelian inheritance'.

lessons.title: DNA structure and how it copies itself
lessons.grammar_note: Base-pairing rule: A–T and G–C. Strands run antiparallel (5′→3′ opposite 3′→5′).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the structure of DNA and explain why replication is called *semiconservative*. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, which base pairs with adenine?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: DNA is a *double helix*: two strands twisted together. Each strand is a chain of *nucleotides*, and each nucleotide has a sugar, a phosphate, and one of four *bases* — adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G), cytosine (C). The two strands are held together by base pairing: A always pairs with T, and G always pairs with C. The strands are *antiparallel* — one runs 5′→3′ while its partner runs 3′→5′. Because each base specifies its partner, one strand is a template for rebuilding the other. That is the whole trick of heredity.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Replication is *semiconservative*: each new double helix keeps one old strand and one new strand. First, the enzyme *helicase* unwinds the helix; then *DNA polymerase* reads each template and adds complementary nucleotides in the 5′→3′ direction. Take the template strand 3′-T A C G G A-5′. Reading the pairing rule (A↔T, G↔C), the new strand is 5′-A T G C C T-3′. Notice every A on the template drew a T, and every G drew a C.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Write the complementary strand for each template. (1) 3′-A A T C-5′ (2) 3′-G C G T-5′ (3) 3′-T T A C G-5′ (4) 3′-C A T G-5′. Answers: (1) 5′-T T A G-3′; (2) 5′-C G C A-3′; (3) 5′-A A T G C-3′; (4) 5′-G T A C-3′.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: pairing A with G or C (only A–T and G–C are allowed). Mistake: thinking both strands are newly built — one is always inherited (that's what 'semiconservative' means). Exit: (a) What pairs with cytosine? (b) After replication, how many original strands are in each new double helix? Answers: guanine; one.

lessons.title: Genes, chromosomes, and mutations
lessons.grammar_note: Gene = a stretch of DNA. Allele = one version of a gene. Humans: 46 chromosomes (23 pairs).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how genes sit on chromosomes and how mutations change them. Warm-up: what do we call one version of a gene?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A *gene* is a segment of DNA that carries instructions for a product, usually a protein. Genes are packaged, wound around proteins, into *chromosomes*. Humans have 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 *homologous pairs* — one of each pair from each parent. Because you inherit a pair, you carry two copies of most genes; different versions of a gene are called *alleles*. A *mutation* is a change in the DNA sequence. A *point mutation* swaps a single base (a substitution); *insertions* or *deletions* add or remove bases and can shift the whole reading frame (a *frameshift*).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Sickle-cell disease comes from a single point mutation in the beta-globin gene: the DNA codon changes from GAG to GTG. That one-base swap changes the amino acid from glutamic acid to valine, and the altered protein makes red blood cells stiffen into a sickle shape. One base out of billions — a big effect. Contrast that with a *silent* mutation, where the base change still codes for the same amino acid and nothing changes.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Classify each mutation. (1) A T→C substitution that still codes for the same amino acid. (2) One base removed, shifting everything downstream. (3) A change from a normal codon to a stop codon. (4) A single base swapped for another, changing one amino acid. Answers: (1) silent point mutation; (2) frameshift (deletion); (3) nonsense mutation; (4) missense point mutation.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking a gene and a chromosome are the same size (a chromosome holds many genes). Mistake: assuming every mutation is harmful — many are silent or even helpful. Exit: (a) How many chromosome pairs do humans have? (b) What is a frameshift caused by? Answers: 23 pairs; an insertion or deletion of bases.

lessons.title: Mendelian inheritance and Punnett squares
lessons.grammar_note: Dominant allele = capital letter; recessive = lowercase. Genotype = the alleles; phenotype = the visible trait.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Use a Punnett square to predict offspring ratios and state Mendel's two laws. Warm-up: what ratio do you expect from crossing two heterozygotes?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Mendel found that traits are passed as discrete units (now called *genes*). Each parent carries two *alleles* and passes one to each offspring — the *law of segregation*. A *dominant* allele (written with a capital, e.g. A) masks a *recessive* one (lowercase, a). *Homozygous* means two identical alleles (AA or aa); *heterozygous* means two different ones (Aa). A *Punnett square* lists each parent's possible gametes on the two sides and fills the boxes with the offspring combinations.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Cross two heterozygous tall pea plants, Aa × Aa. Each parent makes A and a gametes. The 2×2 square gives: AA, Aa, Aa, aa. Genotype ratio 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa. Since A is dominant, AA, Aa, and Aa are all tall and only aa is short — a phenotype ratio of 3 tall : 1 short, i.e. 3:1. Now a *dihybrid* cross, AaBb × AaBb, follows the *law of independent assortment* (genes on different chromosomes sort independently). Its 4×4 square yields the classic 9:3:3:1 phenotype ratio — 9 showing both dominant traits, 3 and 3 showing one each, 1 showing both recessive.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: (1) In Aa × Aa, what fraction of offspring are homozygous recessive? (2) Cross a heterozygote with a homozygous recessive (Aa × aa) — what is the phenotype ratio? (3) In the 9:3:3:1 dihybrid result, how many of 16 boxes show both recessive traits? (4) Two brown-eyed parents (Bb × Bb) have a blue-eyed child (bb) — was that possible? Answers: (1) 1/4; (2) 1:1 (half dominant, half recessive); (3) 1 of 16; (4) yes — each parent can pass the recessive b.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: writing the offspring ratio as the genotype ratio (1:2:1) when the question asks for phenotype (3:1). Mistake: thinking two dominant-looking parents can't have a recessive child (Aa × Aa can). Exit: (a) Phenotype ratio of Aa × Aa? (b) Which law explains the 9:3:3:1 result? Answers: 3:1; the law of independent assortment.

questions.prompt: In DNA, guanine (G) always pairs with…
questions.explanation: G pairs with C.

questions.prompt: 'Semiconservative' replication means each new double helix contains…
options: one old and one new strand
questions.explanation: One template strand is conserved, one is newly made.

questions.prompt: A frameshift mutation is caused by…
options: an insertion or deletion of bases
questions.explanation: Adding or removing bases shifts the reading frame.

questions.prompt: The genotype Aa is described as…
questions.explanation: Two different alleles = heterozygous.

questions.prompt: Crossing Aa × Aa gives a phenotype ratio of…
questions.explanation: 3 dominant : 1 recessive.

questions.prompt: A dihybrid cross AaBb × AaBb produces a phenotype ratio of…
questions.explanation: The classic 9:3:3:1 from independent assortment.

lessons.title: Meiosis and the sources of genetic variation
lessons.grammar_note: Diploid (2n) → meiosis → four haploid (n) gametes. Crossing over happens in prophase I.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how meiosis halves the chromosome number and creates variation. Warm-up: are gametes haploid or diploid?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Body cells are *diploid* (2n): they carry two of each chromosome. To make gametes (eggs and sperm), a cell runs *meiosis* — two rounds of division that produce four *haploid* (n) cells, each with a single set of chromosomes. In humans that means going from 46 chromosomes to 23. When a sperm and egg fuse at fertilization, the diploid number is restored. Two features of meiosis generate variation: *crossing over*, where homologous chromosomes swap segments during prophase I, and the *independent assortment* of homologous pairs during metaphase I.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Consider independent assortment alone. Each of the 23 human chromosome pairs lines up and sorts independently, so the number of possible gamete combinations is 2^23 ≈ 8.4 million — before crossing over adds even more. That is why siblings differ. Contrast meiosis with *mitosis*, which makes two identical diploid cells for growth and repair; meiosis instead makes four genetically unique haploid cells.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: (1) How many haploid cells does one meiosis produce? (2) If a diploid cell has 2n = 8, how many chromosomes are in each gamete? (3) In which phase does crossing over occur? (4) Does mitosis or meiosis create genetic variation? Answers: (1) four; (2) 4; (3) prophase I; (4) meiosis.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing meiosis with mitosis (mitosis = two identical diploid cells; meiosis = four varied haploid cells). Mistake: thinking gametes are diploid. Exit: (a) From 46 chromosomes, how many does a human gamete carry? (b) Name one source of variation in meiosis. Answers: 23; crossing over (or independent assortment).

lessons.title: Transcription and translation: reading the code
lessons.grammar_note: Central dogma: DNA → RNA → protein. A codon is three mRNA bases; AUG = start (methionine).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Trace how a gene becomes a protein through transcription and translation. Warm-up: which base replaces thymine in RNA?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The *central dogma* is DNA → RNA → protein. In *transcription*, the enzyme RNA polymerase reads a DNA template and builds a matching *messenger RNA (mRNA)* strand — but RNA uses *uracil (U)* wherever DNA would use thymine. In *translation*, a *ribosome* reads the mRNA three bases at a time. Each triplet is a *codon* that specifies one amino acid, delivered by *tRNA*. Amino acids link into a protein. Reading starts at the *start codon* AUG (methionine) and ends at a *stop codon*.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Take the DNA template strand 3′-T A C-5′. Transcription pairs it (A↔U, T↔A, G↔C, C↔G) into the mRNA codon 5′-A U G-3′. Look up AUG in the genetic code: it is methionine, the start signal. Next take DNA template 3′-A A A-5′ → mRNA 5′-U U U-3′ → phenylalanine. So the template 3′-TAC-AAA-5′ produces the mRNA AUG-UUU and the peptide Met–Phe.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: (1) In RNA, what pairs with adenine? (2) How many bases make one codon? (3) Transcribe the DNA template 3′-T A C-5′ into mRNA. (4) What amino acid does the codon AUG specify? Answers: (1) uracil; (2) three; (3) 5′-A U G-3′; (4) methionine (the start).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using thymine in RNA (RNA has uracil instead). Mistake: reading codons as two bases instead of three. Exit: (a) What does transcription produce? (b) How many bases in a codon? Answers: messenger RNA (mRNA); three.

items.translation: one of the alternative versions of a gene
items.example: The brown-eye and blue-eye alleles are versions of the same eye-color gene.

items.translation: the specific alleles an organism carries for a trait
items.example: A plant with the genotype Aa is heterozygous.

items.translation: the observable trait produced by the genotype
items.example: The phenotype of an Aa pea plant is tall.

items.translation: having two identical alleles for a gene (AA or aa)
items.example: Only homozygous recessive (aa) plants are short.

items.translation: a sequence of three mRNA bases that codes for one amino acid
items.example: The codon AUG signals the start of translation and codes for methionine.

items.translation: cell division that makes four haploid gametes from a diploid cell
items.example: Meiosis halves the chromosome number, from 46 to 23 in humans.

questions.explanation: Meiosis yields four haploid gametes.

questions.prompt: In RNA, adenine pairs with…
questions.explanation: RNA uses uracil in place of thymine.

questions.prompt: The central dogma of molecular biology is…
questions.explanation: Information flows DNA → RNA → protein.

questions.prompt: The start codon AUG codes for the amino acid…
questions.explanation: AUG codes for methionine and signals the start of translation.

questions.prompt: Crossing over, a source of variation, occurs during…
questions.explanation: Homologous chromosomes swap segments in prophase I.

questions.prompt: A human gamete carries how many chromosomes?
questions.explanation: Gametes are haploid: 23 chromosomes.

lessons.title: Applied project: predict inheritance across generations

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Choose a single-gene trait that follows simple dominant/recessive inheritance (for example: pea plant height, the ability to roll your tongue, or attached vs. free earlobes). You will predict how it is passed down across three generations using Punnett squares — no lab needed, just careful reasoning.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) Define your trait and assign symbols (capital for dominant, lowercase for recessive). 2) Pick starting genotypes for two grandparents and cross them with a Punnett square; report the genotype and phenotype ratios. 3) Choose one offspring, give it a mate, and cross again to predict the grandchildren. 4) State the probability that a specific grandchild shows the recessive phenotype, and explain how a recessive trait can 'skip' a generation.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ Symbols and genotypes are defined clearly and used consistently. ✔ Each Punnett square is filled correctly and the ratios (e.g. 3:1 or 1:1) match the boxes. ✔ Probabilities are stated as fractions or percentages and are internally consistent. ✔ You correctly explained that a recessive allele can be carried by a heterozygote without showing, then reappear when two carriers meet. If all four hold, you've reasoned like a geneticist.
